Below we detailed the gains secured by the base metals from their lows for the year to Friday April 3 official cash settlement price. Al: +12.4%; Cu: +35.4%; Ni +9.6%; Pb +29.3%; Sn +9.3% and Zn +23.9% The increases raise some obvious questions. How much of the improved outlook is already in the price and whether the relative performance of the base metals is a fair reflection of the individual fundamentals. The final question is whether the markets have jumped the gun and that they will be faced with weak demand conditions for much of 2009, and remain heavily reliant on China to continue to support the markets. ### **Fundamentals play their part** In terms of the relative performance of the metals, it does appear to reflect the underlying fundamentals. Aluminium and nickel have rightly lagged behind due to an inadequate supply response to the dramatic collapse in demand. The underperformance of tin is slightly harder to explain, although the restart of Yunnan Tin is hanging over the market. For copper, lead and zinc the inventory accumulation so far this cycle has been relatively small and the supply response for lead and zinc is beginning to kick-in. ### **Is the good news already in the price?** GFMS Metals Consulting believes this to be the case and we would need another tranche of bullish news to support current price levels. In our two Briefing Updates in March we q

uestioned whether the China factor will begin to fade (March 26th) and we commented “Industrial production a reality check (March 17th). This followed on from our previous monthly which was entitled Base metals: China versus the rest of the world. These themes highlight our view that it is bit early to see another significant leg up from current levels. The story for the second quarter is likely to be the extent to which the markets can hold onto Q1 gains. However, one can certainly argue that we have already seen the lows for the metals in this cycle, with the cost curve providing some support for prices. The first quarter was very difficult for manufacturing, but there are tentative signs the pace of contraction is moderating. There has been a sharp reduction in inventories, which should leave the manufacturing sector well placed when underlying demand begins to improve. ### **Will unemployment stymie the recovery?** One problem, not just in the US but in all markets, is the continued rise in unemployment. In March, US employment fell by 633,000, which raised the unemployment rate to 8.5%. Empoyment has fallen by around 3m in the last six months. Partly reflecting the employment position, the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index remains at low levels despite a rise in March to 57.3 compared to 56.3 in February, reflecting an improvement in the expectations component. The improvement in the index however is anemic and is consistent with a deep recession. **4** GFMS METALS CONSULTING METALS CONSULTING ECONOMIC AND DEMAND INDICATORS **GFMS-MC Prices Indices, Jan '02 - Apr '09 (Jan '02 = 100)** 500

### **Europe: Worse before it gets better** The European Commission’s economic sentiment indicator fell to a record low of 64.6 in March well down on its longterm average of 100. Sentiment fell in all the key sectors except for construction and retail. Despite concerted monetary and fiscal efforts, the economy will remain firmly in the grip of recession this year as consumers rein in spending and businesses slash production, investment and staff. There will also be no support from exports, which has been the main driver of growth over recent years. Unemployment in the Euro-zone rose to 8.5% in February up from 8.3% in January and is now at the highest level since April 2006. Most indicators relating both to the domestic and export markets are pointing down suggesting a further rise in unemployment. Fears about job security, will partially offset the stimulus measures taken by the various government and the reduction in rates by the ECB. ### **Japan: Even worse before it gets better** The latest economic releases relating to the Japanese economy are dire for the prospects for base metals demand within the country. The Quarterly Tankan survey of business confidence collapsed in Q1 to -58, the lowest reading since the survey began in 1974. Weakness was seen across the board. The worst affected sector is automotive, which had a reading of -92. Japanese IP fell by 9.4% m-o-m in February and was down nearly 40% y-o-y. One reason for the collapse is the 50% decline in exports. Reflecting the poor conditions in both

home and export markets, Japan’s manufacturing capacity utilization has retreated by more than 30% in the past six months. **5** GFMS METALS CONSULTING METALS CONSULTING OECD Composite Leading Indicator vs.

**6** GFMS METALS CONSULTING METALS CONSULTING SECTION 6: COPPER # **COPPER** Copper prices, in March, gained some momentum averaging $3,750/tonne, 13.1% up from February, stimulated mainly by Chinese buying, the tight scrap market, and some mildly encouraging data relating to the US housing market. March certainly saw increased volatility of 19.2% compared to 11% in February (when measured as the high minus the low over the low price), particularly towards the latter part of the month. Copper has started on positive note at the start of April, currently trading at $4,130/tonne on April 3. ### **Copper registers a larg

e surplus in 2008** According to the International Copper Study Group (ICSG), the copper market registered a 363,000 tonne surplus in 2008, 27% higher from the previous year. The main factor behind this was declining global demand, particularly over the second half of the year; nevertheless the organisation estimates growth of 2.2% to 18.109m tonnes for the year as a whole. Global consumption growth was mainly driven by China, where apparent consumption grew by 14%. Excluding China, the growth actually fell by 2% due to depressed demand in Europe, the US and Japan, where demand declined by 6%, 8.7% and 5.4%, respectively. The annual figures hide the collapse in demand in Q4. Global consumption in December at 1.40m tonnes was 9% down on October. ### **Chinese demand rockets in February…** China’s implied copper demand surged nearly 44% from the previous month to 591,000 tonnes in February on the back of record high imports. Year-to-date (y-t-d), the country imported just over 1m tonnes of the red metal in all forms. The breakdown by product is as follows: concentrates (266,000 tonnes), refined metal (451,000 tonnes) and scrap (402,000 tonnes). ### **Global mine production sees no change in 2008** According to the ICSG, global mine production remained flat at 15.458m tonnes in 2008; concentrate production was down by 0.9% while SX-EW output was up around 3.5%. Supply disruptions over the last year resulted in stagnant production levels that did not keep pace with capacity growth. As a result, utilisation rates fell to 82.3% compared to 85.1% in 2007. Mine output was up in Africa (+13%), down in the Americas (-1%) and practically unchanged in Asia, Europe and Oceania. ### **…however global refined production still** ### **experiences some growth** Global refined production increased by +2.6% in 2008 to reach 18.472m tonnes. Within this, primary production was up by 3.2% while secondary production was down 1%. Not surprisingly, China was the largest contributor to growth (+9.4%) due to expansion at existing refined capacity. On an annual basis, refined output was down in Africa (-3.5%) and North America (-1.1%), but up in all remaining regions; Latin America (+4.7%), Asia (+2.2%), Europe (+3%) and Oceania (+14%). ### **Japan will continue to cutback production** With prices hovering around $4,000/tonne, we do not expect any further cuts in mine production in the near future. However weak demand, a relatively strong yen, low TCs and low by-product prices are putting pressure on Japanese smelters, despite higher exports which increased by +46% y-o-y in February to 65,380 tonnes on the back of strong demand from China. Mitsubishi Materials will continue to curb output at its Japanese smelters over Q2 and Q3 by 10%. itomo Mining plans to produce 401,000 tonnes of copper in the year to end March 2010, up 1.8% y-o-y as earlier production had been curtailed due to maintenance shutdowns. 

### **Latin American production is mixed** 

Lower mine production in Latin America is the key driver behind the tightness in the concentrate market with a 3.3% fall to 7.22m tonnes in 2008.  Sharp delcines in Chile (-4.1%) and Mexico (-26.8%) offset the 6.6% increase in Peru.  This year, we might see a reversal of these trends. 

In Peru, copper production fell by 2.6% y-o-y to 97,685 tonnes in February on declines at two of the country’s largest mines, Cia Minera Antamina and Freeport McMoran’s Cerro Verde.  Similarly, Chilean output declined by 9.8% y-o-y at 393,057 tonnes. 

According to the central bank, Zambian copper production rose by 36% y-o-y to 133,328 tonnes in the first two months of the year.  Elsewhere in the African Copperbelt, Gecamines is looking to boost output to 40,000 tpy by the end of the year from the current 25,000 tpy.  More importantly, cathode production has started at Tenke Fungurume, which should eventually produce at a rate of 115,000 tpy. 

### **Market outlook** 

Views on the copper market appear to be diverging.  The “bulls” suggest that Chinese buying will remain strong reflecting SRB purchases and relatively strong underlying demand.  This should “tie the copper market over” until

there is a recovery in consumption outside of the country. On the supply side, a tight scrap and concentrate market will constrain refined output.  Such a scenario can support a +$4,000/tonne price. 

The “bear” case is that the Chinese buying will prove to be temporary in that SRB purchases may dry up due to the high price levels.  In addition, some of the imports associated with the arbitrage that higher Chinese prices offer have gone into unreported inventory.  Copper inventories have been rising despite the SRB purchases.  Therefore, once this support is removed, the poor underlying fundamentals i.e. weak demand will reassert themselves.  Under this scenario the downside is significant.  We tend to be in the bear camp but reflecting the strong performance in Q1 we have raised our average price this year to $3,500/tonne.  We doubt, however, whether prices will fall much below the January 23 low of $3,051/tonne.

Although more organisations are moving towards a global balance there are “pros and cons” of both methods. The net East West trade flow better captures changes in stockpiles in countries such as China. We plan to continue producing market balances in both forms. Normally the conclusions should be roughly in line. We will, however, highlight any major discrepancies between these two approaches as and when they occur. - The main theme of the copper market in 2008 was demand weakness and supply tightness, with the latter dominating in H1 and the former in H2. There is no sign of demand picking up in the USA. In fact, the weakness that has been present in the housing and autos sectors is now spreading to non-residential construction. On a geographic basis, we note an easing of conditions in the EU and Japan. Most important is the sharp slowdown in demand in China and to a lesser extent the other emerging markets. Anecdotal evidence, low physical premiums, together with the poor economic indicators does not imply a quick rebound in demand. - On the supply side, although continued disruptions and problems with lower grades is keeping the market reasonably tight, this feature is being ignored by the market in the current weak demand environment. The focus is on the fact that copper prices in early 2009 are still only just below the marginal cost of production. The experience of all the other base metals suggest that prices will inevitably fall below this level as inventories rise. - As a result, we believe that copper prices could still fall from the levels of around $4,000/tonne in early April 2009. We are projecting that prices will bottom around $3,000/tonne in 2009 H1, and that prices will average $3,500/tonne compared to last year’s outturn of $6,952/tonne. **18** GFMS METALS CONSULTING METALS CONSULTING COPPER |**Co**|**pper sup**|**ply-dema**

**19** GFMS METALS CONSULTING SECTION 7: NICKEL & COBALT # **NICKEL** As we have noted in our Executive Summary the performance has lagged behind most of the rest of the sector and that this is a fair reflection of the current state of the fundamentals. For most of March, the nickel cash quote traded in a narrow range based around $9,500-9,800/tonne, averaging $9,696/ tonne. This was however almost 7% lower than February and close to the cycle low of $9,686/tonne in December. With the exception of nickel and tin, all the other base metals saw an increase in their March monthly averages. Nonetheless, nickel has started on a more positive note in April, jumping to over $10,800/tonne on April 6, the highest level since mid February. ### **WBMS data highlight the weak demand in 2008…** The main problem facing the nickel industry is the weak demand. The WBMS data confirms the impact of lower stainless output on nickel demand. Offtake in December is estimated at 91,600 tonnes, down 28.5% from the peak of 128,100 tonnes in June. The weakness was carried over to 2009 and consumption in January is estimated at 96,000 tonnes, 16% lower y-o-y. With the exception of Asia, all regions quoted by the organisation experienced declines in exceeding 20% y-o-y

. The steepest fall (-32.7%) was seen in Europe. Asian consumption was just 2.1% down y-o-y. Having increased by 2.2% in 2008, US nickel consumption declined by almost 30% in January, highlighting the dire conditions surrounding the market. Reflecting the weakness, nickel premiums in the country have declined after holding steady since late last year. Premiums are presently in a range of 30-40c/lb for melting grade nickel, down slightly from 32-42c/lb in February. Nickel daily stocks vs price

Given that the cuts in stainless steel remain in place, we could see a y-o-y decline of up to 40% in Q1 as the year earlier was a period of relatively high production of 7.584m tonnes. Despite the production cutbacks, stainless steel prices remain under pressure. For example, Taiwan’s Tang Eng has further lowered output and cut its 304 export price for April by $30-50/tonne as demand remains weak. It has reduced its operating rate to 60-70% of its usual 350,000 tpy capacity in March, down from 80% seen in February. Finnish producer, Outokumpu, has announced that it is temporarily idling around one third of production capacity at its Tornio works. The mills in Europe, which have slashed output, are however looking for an increase in base prices. However, underlying demand conditions remain poor. ### **Supply reductions lose momentum** Obviously the supply response has so far been inadequate with inventories still rising. There were not any further major cuts in output in March, and most of the supply news has related to higher production levels in the future; herein lies the problem for the nickel industry. The most recent cuts have been focused on eastern Europe. Ferronickeli, the Kosovan producer, has cut output back by 50% to 330 tonnes per month. In Russia, Ufaleynickel, which restarted three of its five furnaces (closed since October 2008) in February, has shut down one the furnaces with the potential for further shutdowns in Q2. Production last year was around 10,000 tonnes compared 14,114 tonnes in 2007. Output this year could struggle to reach 7,000 tonnes. Much of the extra nickel production in the future will come from Brazil. Mirabella Nickel has confirmed that the Santa Rita nickel sulphide project is 85% complete, and production is set to commence in the middle of this year. In Australia, BHP Billiton has signed a heads of agreement to secure up to 10,000 tpy of nickel in concentrate from Western Areas. The company’s Flying Fox mine has reached its capacity of 300,000 tpy of ore earlier in the Q1. Last year, the operation produced 8,114 tonnes of nickel. out the prospects for nickel prices for some time having forecast an average price of $9,500/ tonne for Q1.  Although the outcome was slightly higher than this, we see little reason for a sustained rally.  This will require further production cuts and an improvement in nickel demand, which seems some way away given the latest developments in the stainless steel sector. In terms of our projections for 2009, we forecast that the market will be in a surplus of 18,000 tonnes in 2009, down from 33,000 tonnes in 2008.  Given that LME inventories have increased by around 25,000 tonnes so far this year, this implies that the upturn in inventories should be reversed in H2.  For Q2, GFMS Metals Consulting forecasts that prices will average $9,750/tonne, which is below the level prevailing in early April of above $10,000/tonne.  The key driver of the market in the short term will be the continued poor offtake from the stainless steel sector.  However, we expect a sharp rebound in stainless production in Q4 that should allow nickel prices to average $11,250/tonne and we expect that prices could test $14,000/tonne in this period.

# **COBALT** 

Cobalt prices have increased sharply over the last month with high grade material in early April trading a $14.5-16.5/lb up from the previous range of $13-15/lb, and compared to $11-13/lb at the end of February.  The price of 99.3% has risen from $9.9-12.3/lb at the beginning of March to a current range of $13.0-14.7/lb.  The narrowing of the range for low grade material reflects the absence of competitively priced material 

We expect that the rally will begin to run out of steam as demand conditions remain weak.  Even in China, only modest growth is forecast for this year.  A leading producer, Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt Corp, suggests that cobalt consumption will rise by 3-4% in 2009, with increase being driven by the battery and catalyst sectors.  This follows a 5.3% increase to 13,519 tonnes in 2008. The biggest growth market in 2008 was the cobalt lithium oxide industry, which consumed some 5,478 tonnes of cobalt metal last year. 

The company plans to invest around $100m to build a new cobalt tetroxide, which should have a capacity of 5,000 tpy of cobalt.  The plant that will supply the battery market (lithium) and should be completed by early 2010. 

Chambishi Metals, Zambia’s largest cobalt producer, could resume operations in the country, which were halted in December once its secures concentrate contracts.  The company expects to conclude negotiations with potential suppliers of cobalt concentrate from Zambia, as well as the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in time to restart o

perations in May. The move reflects both higher prices and the lifting of a mineral export ban by the Katanga province in the DRC. Reflecting the closure of Chambishi, Zambia’s cobalt production fell 35.8% year-on-year to 251 tonnes in January. Cobalt prices

# **NICKEL SUPPLY-DEMAND BALANCE AND PRICE PROJECTIONS** 

- GFMS Metals Consulting analyses the market balance on both a Western World and global basis.  Although more organisations are moving towards a global balance there are “pros and cons” of both methods. The net East West trade flow better captures changes in stockpiles in countries such as China.  We plan to continue producing market balances in both forms. Normally the conclusions should be roughly in line. We will, however, highlight any major discrepancies between these two approaches as and when they occur. 

- All aspects of the nickel market are in a state of flux in late 2008 - not just the price.  The LME cash quote has fallen by over 80% from its bull market peak, which perhaps not surprisingly has triggered a spate of production cutbacks, particularly among the high-cost nickel pig iron producers in China.  Lower production has also been seen in Australia and  the Dominican Republic. 

- Another supply t

rend is reining back in capital expenditure on projects that are under development that will inevitably delay the commissioning of these projects.

- Despite these developments there is still the potential for a significant surge in production next year if some of the production losses such as the maintenance shutdown at BHP Billiton’s Kalgoorlie plant are added back in and as production is ramped up at Posco 30,000 tpy plant that has just been commissioned.  In addition, there will extra output from the mega projects such as Goro and Onca Puma, even if production will be well below initial expectations in the early phase. 

- At this stage without further additional cuts in capacity we have the nickel market still being in a surplus in 2009.  We believe that this will lead to another downward leg in nickel prices  with average prices falling below $10,000/tonne in Q2.  For the year as a whole, we project an average of $10,495/ tonne. 

# **COBALT SUPPLY-DEMAND BALANCE AND PRICE PROJECTIONS** 

- The performance of the cobalt price is somewhat similar to that of its sister metal, nickel, in that prices have fallen sharply from the bull market peaks, when prices briefly exceeded $50/lb.  The main reason for the correction has been higher production of cobalt (normally in the form of concentrate) from the DRC.  This has led to a surplus of material developing in the key Chinese market. 

- However, the move towards $10/lb has prompted a supply response in Africa.  Such has been tha extent of the decline that the market is now in reasonable balance for 2009.  We are projecting an average price of $14/lb down from $39/lb in 2008.
